title: Hearing shapes: the Bouba–Kiki effect in adult domestic dogs
short_title: Hearing shapes: the Bouba–Kiki effect in dogs

journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
abstract: The ‘Bouba–Kiki effect’ is an example of spontaneous association between auditory and visual stimuli, described in humans as a case of sound symbolism, a predisposition linked to language. Recent evidence showed that 3-day-old chicks also exhibit a spontaneous association between round and spiky shapes and the sounds ‘Bouba’ and ‘Kiki,’ respectively, thus suggesting that the effect may rather be an instance of a more widespread cross-modal correspondence. We investigated whether the Bouba–Kiki effect is present in adult domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) by investigating dogs’ spontaneous tendency to associate a spiky or a rounded shape to the ‘Bouba’ and ‘Kiki’ sounds. Dogs looked significantly more at the rounded shape while ‘Bouba’ was played, and they looked at and explored the spiky shape when ‘Kiki’ was played. Our results suggest that a spontaneous sound–shape association akin to that of humans is also present in adult domestic dogs. Further studies are needed to investigate the function and ontogenesis of this cognitive process.
summary: People often associate the sound “Bouba” with a rounded shape and “Kiki” with a spiky one. We tested whether adult dogs show a similar preference, using video-based gaze analysis and observations of exploration. Dogs looked longer at the matching shape in both a 51-dog study and a 19-dog study whose owners could not hear the sounds. The findings suggest a sound–shape association beyond humans; how it develops and what function it serves remain open questions.
key_findings: Dogs looked longer at rounded shapes during “Bouba” and spiky shapes during “Kiki” in both studies.
The looking preference persisted when owners wore headphones and could not hear the experimental sounds.
Increased exploration of the spiky shape during “Kiki” appeared in Study 1 but was not replicated in Study 2.
Further work is needed to establish the development and function of this cross-modal association.
